bull_bear.body:
- Net-debt-free; gross debt ₹60 cr (₹35 cr LT + ₹25 cr ST); cash ₹40–55 cr. "As good as nil."
- Funding for doubling: "majorly internal accruals or maybe debt"; **no equity dilution** confirmed.
- Renewable capex ₹125 cr (₹115 cr + ₹9 cr), of which only ~₹40 cr debt, rest own funds; ~₹18–20 cr/yr power savings → ~6-yr payback.
- Non-core: ₹1 cr equity stake in **Attero Recycling** — "purely equity investment," not strategic; reiterated focus on core business only.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation (IPO proceeds / balance sheet)

bull_bear.body:
- **Demand/seasonality:** Q3 realisation flattered by winter higher-GSM mix — could moderate in summer.
- **Capex execution:** large multi-year loom build, land acquisition (~300 looms), approvals timing.
- **Geographic concentration:** all 4 units in Surat (mgmt defends as the MMF hub — "Manchester of synthetic fabric"; no plan to diversify).
- **Competition (Surat):** highly fragmented small/less-integrated peers — mgmt claims scale insulation but pricing discipline depends on yarn-price stability.
- **Subsidy roll-off:** power/interest subsidies expiring 2026–28; renewables must land on time (Feb-26 & May-26) to offset.
- **Export/policy:** EU GSP suspension removed Indian textile export benefit; impact indirect via buyers; RM dependence on Chinese yarn (policy-sensitive).
bull_bear.title: Risks

bull_bear.body: Confident, granular, candid (maiden call). Comfortable giving hard numbers (capex ₹35 cr, ₹350–400 cr; debt split; payback; subsidy %s; realisation/util). Repeatedly downplays competition and concentration risk ("not a challenge at all"). Some transcript garbling but substance clear.
bull_bear.title: Management tone

bull_bear.body:
- Texturised yarn (~7%) is deliberate **redundancy capacity** (loom-downtime insurance), not a growth segment — surplus is opportunistically sold.
- Wide 105" looms create a util optic: single-width (bedsheet/shirting) orders show lower utilisation % yet run 100% efficient — utilisation % understates true output.
- The Dec-25 policy change is removal of a **BIS-certificate import restriction** on Chinese yarn (not an anti-dumping duty per se) → *cheaper* RM (gross-margin positive), a nuance vs typical import-substitution framing.
- Subsidy roll-off vs renewables is a deliberate margin-bridge: power savings (~₹20 cr/yr) sized to replace expiring power subsidy.
- ₹1 cr Attero stake is immaterial and explicitly disowned as a strategy — pre-empts any "diversification" read.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- integration: in-house texturising and twisting feed the majority of fabric produced — evidence: '99% Fabric enabled by in-house texturising and twisting'
- customer lock-in: high share of repeat business — evidence: '98% Repeat orders, reflecting enduring customer confidence'
- scale: production capacity has grown substantially over five years — evidence: '7x Production-capacity growth between 2021 and 2026' [planned, partly reflects the ongoing Unit 4 expansion]
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Raw material price risk — The company is dependent on key raw materials such as yarn, dyes and chemicals; volatility from market imbalances, climatic conditions or geopolitical developments can impact production costs and operating margins.
- Competitive intensity risk — The Indian textile sector competes with both domestic and international manufacturers; increased competition from low-cost manufacturing countries and changing global sourcing patterns may pressure pricing, market share and profitability.
- Foreign exchange risk — Fluctuations in foreign currency exchange rates may impact export realizations, import costs and overall competitiveness in global markets.
- Global economic and market risk — Macroeconomic uncertainties, inflationary pressures, geopolitical conflicts and fluctuations in consumer spending patterns across major economies may affect demand for textile and apparel products.
- Regulatory and sustainability compliance risk — Increasing environmental, social and governance regulatory requirements globally may require continuous investment in technology, systems and processes.
- Supply chain and logistics risk — Disruptions from geopolitical tensions, transportation constraints, raw material shortages or global trade disturbances may impact operational continuity and delivery schedules.
- Energy and utility cost risk — Manufacturing operations require significant power, fuel and water consumption; substantial increases in utility costs may affect operational efficiency and cost competitiveness.
- Technology and innovation risk — Rapid advancements in manufacturing technologies, automation and digitalization require continuous modernization; failure to adopt emerging technologies may affect productivity, product quality and competitive positioning.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body: Polyester yarn demand "improved" and pricing "stabilized" over past months → reduced value-chain volatility, better volume visibility. PFY ~80% of India's MMF production. Borana's product is the base for dyeing/printing/finishing across apparel, home furnishings, technical textiles (tents, hospital linens, waterproof, jackets). Domestic demand easily absorbs production; export upside is *indirect* via buyers (US bedsheet demand softened; shifted to UAE/Middle East — versatile looms re-tooled accordingly).

- **Texturised yarn** — ~7% of sales; deliberately over-built capacity as insurance against loom downtime; surplus sold but "not part of the business to sell yarn." Not the same 2–3x asset turn.

- ✅ Anti-dumping probe on imported textured/partially-oriented yarn supports domestic yarn/fabric pricing discipline (structural positive for the value chain).

business.title: Competitive strengths

latest_quarter.body:
- RM (polyester yarn) cost "not that much fluctuating"; Dec-25 removal of BIS curb on Chinese yarn → cheaper imports, Q4 gross-margin tailwind. Mgmt confident of competing with China even at parity RM (Indian power cost similar, Chinese wages higher).
- Power/fuel/labour structurally low; bulk RM procurement aids cost + supply reliability.
- **State subsidies (rolling off):** interest subsidy ~3–4% (≈30–40% of interest cost) + power subsidy ₹2/unit (~20–22%), 5-yr per unit — Unit1 to 2026, Unit2 to 2027, Unit3 to 2028. Renewable rollout intended to offset subsidy expiry so "margin not affected at all."
latest_quarter.title: Margins & cost

latest_quarter.body: - **Q3 FY26 (maiden call, baseline):** Rev ₹111.36 cr (+42% YoY); EBITDA ₹27.09 cr (+51%, 24.32% margin); PAT ₹18.55 cr (+63%). Volume 6.60 cr m (9M 16.31 cr m). Util ~82–83% (max ~90%). Net-debt-free. Capacity 39.21 cr m / ~1,000 looms; Unit 4B 64/160 looms live (+5 cr m/yr, ₹35 cr). Guidance: double to 2,000 looms by Mar-28 (1,500 by FY27), ₹350–400 cr, no dilution; renewables ₹125 cr → ~₹20 cr/yr savings (Feb-26 & May-26); realisation ₹16+/sq m sustainable; value-add 20–25%; yarn 7%. One-offs: winter higher-GSM mix lift; other income down to ₹1.6 cr (no Unit-3 subsidy lump); Chinese-yarn BIS curb removed Dec-25 (Q4 GM tailwind).
latest_quarter.title: QoQ Log

outlook.body:
- **Volume / realisation:** Realisation to stay on "positive side," ~₹16+/sq m sustainable (vs ₹15.80 FY25); volume to rise with new loom commissioning.
- **Capacity ramp (new looms):** Unit 4B = ~160 new high-speed water-jet looms; 64 commissioned, **balance starting February 2026**. Adds ~5 cr metres/yr (₹60–75 cr incremental annual revenue, fully utilised by next year). Project cost ~₹35 cr.
- **Capacity DOUBLING:** 1,000 → 2,000 looms by **March 2028**; interim exit ~1,500 looms by FY27-end. Total investment ₹350–400 cr (≈₹200 cr capex + ₹50–70 cr working capital + renewables). Land available for ~700 looms; need to buy for ~300 (approvals "not a challenge").
- **Margin:** EBITDA margin to "gradually increase" QoQ as new machines complete (lower depreciation drag, falling interest cost); 25–25.5% aspirational but ~23–24% base. Q4 gross margin may beat Q3 on cheaper Chinese RM.
- **Value-add:** ~20–25% of production is value-added today; churned opportunistically with demand-supply, no fixed target. Texturised yarn ~7% of sales (kept as buffer capacity, sold as surplus, not a strategic line).
- **POY:** Backward integration into POY manufacturing only *after* capacity doubling.
outlook.title: Guidance (CRITICAL)

outlook.body:
- Capacity doubling 1,000→2,000 looms (Mar-28); interim 1,500 (FY27).
- Renewables to structurally lower power cost (largest controllable cost lever).
- Technical-textile *fabric* base (tents, hospital linens, jackets, waterproof) — Borana supplies fabric; buyers do coating. Capacity added "slowly and gradually," demand-led, no fixed capex.
- Optional forward into POY manufacturing post-doubling.
- Export optionality (indirect) — versatile water-jet looms re-configurable per destination/fabric.
outlook.title: Growth / optionality

outlook.body:
- Strengthen the core greige-fabric manufacturing business while enhancing capacity utilisation and improving cost efficiencies.
- Explore value-added and man-made fibre-based textile products beyond conventional greige fabric.
- Growth strategy centred on greater productivity, operational excellence and responsible resource use rather than capacity addition alone.
- Continue modernising facilities, installing high-speed water-jet looms and adopting advanced manufacturing technologies.
- Improve manufacturing efficiency, reduce waste and strengthen renewable energy use.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: The Company is executing a Unit 4 expansion, adding 192 high-speed water-jet looms and 3 texturising machines, with commercial production targeted for December 2026. This follows a broader multi-year capacity build-out — the Company states production capacity has grown 7x between 2021 and 2026 — across its four integrated manufacturing units (POY-to-PTY texturising, warping, sizing and weaving) at Sachin, Surat, Gujarat.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- India's water-jet loom fabric production is projected to grow from 12.1 billion metres in 2025 to over 18.5 billion metres by 2031.
- Demand supported by government initiatives such as PM MITRA Parks, PLI Scheme for Textiles, and China Plus One sourcing shifts favouring India.
- Political crisis in Bangladesh has opened new avenues for Indian textile manufacturers as global buyers seek stable supply chains.
- Consumer preferences are steadily shifting towards man-made fibres, a trend the Company sees as an opportunity given its established polyester fabric platform.
- Gujarat remains the dominant hub of India's textile and weaving manufacturing capacity.
- Industry outlook tempered by a fragmented, SME-heavy structure and rising freight/logistics costs pressuring margins.
outlook.title: Demand & outlook drivers

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Borana Weaves Limited is an integrated, technology-led manufacturer of high-quality microfilament woven greige fabric, spanning POY-to-PTY texturising, warping, sizing and weaving across four manufacturing units.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Borana Weaves manufactures synthetic and blended greige fabric through an integrated process from polymer yarn (POY) through texturising, warping and water-jet weaving to finished greige fabric. The fabric serves apparel, home textiles and tent-fabric applications, with specialised bleaching, dyeing, printing and finishing unlocking colour and application diversity.

segment_detail.title: Segment (fabric / yarn)
segment_detail.body:
- **Grey fabric** — core ~93% of sales; unbleached synthetic grey, sold to Surat process houses then distributed across India/world. Asset turnover ~2–3x.
- **Texturised yarn** — ~7% of sales; deliberately over-built capacity as insurance against loom downtime; surplus sold but "not part of the business to sell yarn." Not the same 2–3x asset turn.

products.title: Products & brands
products.body:
- **Greige fabric:** Synthetic and blended greige fabric
- **End-use applications:** Apparel fabric, Home textiles (bedding and furnishing), Tent fabrics

end_markets.title: End Markets (RHP)
end_markets.body:
- Apparel
- Home textiles
- Tent fabrics / technical textiles

guidance.title: Guidance (CRITICAL)
guidance.body:
- **Volume / realisation:** Realisation to stay on "positive side," ~₹16+/sq m sustainable (vs ₹15.80 FY25); volume to rise with new loom commissioning.
- **Capacity ramp (new looms):** Unit 4B = ~160 new high-speed water-jet looms; 64 commissioned, **balance starting February 2026**. Adds ~5 cr metres/yr (₹60–75 cr incremental annual revenue, fully utilised by next year). Project cost ~₹35 cr.
- **Capacity DOUBLING:** 1,000 → 2,000 looms by **March 2028**; interim exit ~1,500 looms by FY27-end. Total investment ₹350–400 cr (≈₹200 cr capex + ₹50–70 cr working capital + renewables). Land available for ~700 looms; need to buy for ~300 (approvals "not a challenge").
- **Margin:** EBITDA margin to "gradually increase" QoQ as new machines complete (lower depreciation drag, falling interest cost); 25–25.5% aspirational but ~23–24% base. Q4 gross margin may beat Q3 on cheaper Chinese RM.
- **Value-add:** ~20–25% of production is value-added today; churned opportunistically with demand-supply, no fixed target. Texturised yarn ~7% of sales (kept as buffer capacity, sold as surplus, not a strategic line).
- **POY:** Backward integration into POY manufacturing only *after* capacity doubling.

growth_optionality.title: Growth / optionality
growth_optionality.body:
- Capacity doubling 1,000→2,000 looms (Mar-28); interim 1,500 (FY27).
- Renewables to structurally lower power cost (largest controllable cost lever).
- Technical-textile *fabric* base (tents, hospital linens, jackets, waterproof) — Borana supplies fabric; buyers do coating. Capacity added "slowly and gradually," demand-led, no fixed capex.
- Optional forward into POY manufacturing post-doubling.
- Export optionality (indirect) — versatile water-jet looms re-configurable per destination/fabric.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- India's water-jet loom fabric production is projected to grow from 12.1 billion metres in 2025 to over 18.5 billion metres by 2031.
- Demand supported by government initiatives such as PM MITRA Parks, PLI Scheme for Textiles, and China Plus One sourcing shifts favouring India.
- Political crisis in Bangladesh has opened new avenues for Indian textile manufacturers as global buyers seek stable supply chains.
- Consumer preferences are steadily shifting towards man-made fibres, a trend the Company sees as an opportunity given its established polyester fabric platform.
- Gujarat remains the dominant hub of India's textile and weaving manufacturing capacity.
- Industry outlook tempered by a fragmented, SME-heavy structure and rising freight/logistics costs pressuring margins.

themes.need: India textiles ride three tailwinds at once: China+1 sourcing shifts, the India-UK FTA (signed) + India-EU FTA (advancing), and US tariff normalization - favouring apparel exporters (GOKEX/PGIL/PDSL) and US-heavy home-textile names (WELSPUNLIV/HIMATSEIDE). A second leg = value-added synthetics/recycling (FILATEX, SANATHAN, CENTENKA, GANECOS) and cotton-yarn spread recovery (VTL/NITINSPIN/SPORTKING) plus branded apparel (PAGEIND, ARVIND, RAYMONDLSL).
themes.driver: FTA implementation + US-India trade-deal clarity; festive/wedding demand; cotton-yarn spread; anti-dumping rulings.
